    <meta name="dc.description" content="Automatic genre identification (AGI) is a text classification task focused on genres, i.e., text categories defined by the author’s purpose, common function of the text, and the text’s conventional form. Obtaining genre information has been shown to be beneficial for a wide range of disciplines, including linguistics, corpus linguistics, computational linguistics, natural language processing, information retrieval and information security. Consequently, in the past 20 years, numerous researchers have collected genre datasets with the aim to develop an efficient genre classifier. However, their approaches to the definition of genre schemata, data collection and manual annotation vary substantially, resulting in significantly different datasets. As most AGI experiments are dataset-dependent, a sufficient understanding of the differences between the available genre datasets is of great importance for the researchers venturing into this area. In this paper, we present a detailed overview of different approaches to each of the steps of the AGI task, from the definition of the genre concept and the genre schema, to the dataset collection and annotation methods, and, finally, to machine learning strategies. Special focus is dedicated to the description of the most relevant genre schemata and datasets, and details on the availability of all of the datasets are provided. In addition, the paper presents the recent advances in machine learning approaches to automatic genre identification, and concludes with proposing the directions towards developing a stable multilingual genre classifier.">

    <meta property="og:title" content="Automatic genre identification: a survey - Language Resources and Evaluation">
    <meta property="og:description" content="Automatic genre identification (AGI) is a text classification task focused on genres, i.e., text categories defined by the author’s purpose, common function of the text, and the text’s conventional form. Obtaining genre information has been shown to be beneficial for a wide range of disciplines, including linguistics, corpus linguistics, computational linguistics, natural language processing, information retrieval and information security. Consequently, in the past 20 years, numerous researchers have collected genre datasets with the aim to develop an efficient genre classifier. However, their approaches to the definition of genre schemata, data collection and manual annotation vary substantially, resulting in significantly different datasets. As most AGI experiments are dataset-dependent, a sufficient understanding of the differences between the available genre datasets is of great importance for the researchers venturing into this area. In this paper, we present a detailed overview of different approaches to each of the steps of the AGI task, from the definition of the genre concept and the genre schema, to the dataset collection and annotation methods, and, finally, to machine learning strategies. Special focus is dedicated to the description of the most relevant genre schemata and datasets, and details on the availability of all of the datasets are provided. In addition, the paper presents the recent advances in machine learning approaches to automatic genre identification, and concludes with proposing the directions towards developing a stable multilingual genre classifier.">

Consequently, in the past 20 years, numerous researchers have collected genre datasets with the aim to develop an efficient genre classifier. However, their approaches to the definition of genre schemata, data collection and manual annotation vary substantially, resulting in significantly different datasets. As most AGI experiments are dataset-dependent, a sufficient understanding of the differences between the available genre datasets is of great importance for the researchers venturing into this area.                     <section aria-labelledby="Abs1" data-title="Abstract" lang="en"><div class="c-article-section" id="Abs1-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Abs1">Abstract</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Abs1-content"><p>Automatic genre identification (AGI) is a text classification task focused on genres, i.e., text categories defined by the author’s purpose, common function of the text, and the text’s conventional form. Obtaining genre information has been shown to be beneficial for a wide range of disciplines, including linguistics, corpus linguistics, computational linguistics, natural language processing, information retrieval and information security. Consequently, in the past 20 years, numerous researchers have collected genre datasets with the aim to develop an efficient genre classifier. However, their approaches to the definition of genre schemata, data collection and manual annotation vary substantially, resulting in significantly different datasets. As most AGI experiments are dataset-dependent, a sufficient understanding of the differences between the available genre datasets is of great importance for the researchers venturing into this area. In this paper, we present a detailed overview of different approaches to each of the steps of the AGI task, from the definition of the genre concept and the genre schema, to the dataset collection and annotation methods, and, finally, to machine learning strategies. Special focus is dedicated to the description of the most relevant genre schemata and datasets, and details on the availability of all of the datasets are provided. In addition, the paper presents the recent advances in machine learning approaches to automatic genre identification, and concludes with proposing the directions towards developing a stable multilingual genre classifier.</p></div></div></section>

                                    <section data-title="Introduction"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec1-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec1"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">1 </span>Introduction</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec1-content"><p>Genres are text categories, defined by the author’s purpose, common function of the text, and the text’s conventional form (Orlikowski & Yates, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1994" title="Orlikowski, W. J., & Yates, J. (1994). Genre repertoire: The structuring of communicative practices in organizations. Administrative Science Quarterly, 5, 541–574." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR69" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e453">1994</a>). They have been studied already in Antiquity, as the Greek philosophers and orators recognized that the manner in which the information is conveyed plays an important role on the receivers’ understanding of the message, as well as the efficiency of communication (Kwasnik & Crowston, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2005" title="Kwaśnik, B. H., & Crowston, K. (2005). Introduction to the special issue: Genres of digital documents. Information Technology & People." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR49" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e456">2005</a>). As genre involves multiple discourse, language and textual phenomena, it has been studied by researchers from various fields. The term is widely used in linguistics, rhetoric, literary theory, discourse studies, media theory, as well as computational linguistics and information retrieval studies (Chandler, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1997" title="Chandler, D. (1997). An introduction to genre theory." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR15" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e459">1997</a>). The importance of providing information on genres included in a text collection was also recognized by the authors of reference corpora, such as the British National Corpus (BNC) (Davies, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Davies, M. (2004). British National Corpus (from Oxford University Press). Available online at 
                  https://www.english-corpora.org/ bnc/
                  
                " href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR19" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e462">2004</a>) and the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA) (Davies, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2008" title="Davies, M. (2008). The Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA). Available online at 
                  https://www.english-corpora.org/ coca/
                  
                " href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR20" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e465">2008</a>).</p><p>Since the advent of the World Wide Web, there has been an increased interest in identifying genres in text collections, as the web allowed querying and collecting unprecedented quantities of texts. There has been large interest in genre identification in the area of information retrieval (see Stubbe and Ringlstetter <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Stubbe, A., & Ringlstetter, C. (2007). Recognizing genres. Towards a reference corpus of web genres: Proceedings." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR98" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e471">2007</a>; Eissen and Stein <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Zu Eissen, S.M., & Stein, B. (2004). Genre classification of web pages. In: Annual Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 256–269." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR109" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e474">2004</a>; Vidulin et al. <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Vidulin, V., Luštrek, M., & Gams, M. (2007). Using genres to improve search engines. In: 1st International Workshop: Towards Genre-Enabled Search Engines: The Impact of Natural Language Processing, pp. 45–51." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR105" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e477">2007</a>; Roussinov et al. <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2001" title="Roussinov, D., Crowston, K., Nilan, M., Kwasnik, B., Cai, J., & Liu, X. (2001). Genre based navigation on the web. In: Proceedings of the 34th annual Hawaii international conference on system sciences, p. 10." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR82" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e480">2001</a>; Finn and Kushmerick <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2006" title="Finn, A., & Kushmerick, N. (2006). Learning to classify documents according to genre. Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 57(11), 1506–1518." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR27" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e483">2006</a>; Boese <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2005" title="Boese, E.S. (2005). Stereotyping the web: Genre classification of web documents (Unpublished doctoral dissertation). Citeseer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR13" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e487">2005</a>; Priyatam et al. <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2013" title="Priyatam, P. N., Iyengar, S., Perumal, K., & Varma, V. (2013). Don’t use a lot when little will do: Genre identification using URLs. Research in Computing Science, 70, 233–243." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR74" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e490">2013</a>; Stein et al. <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Stein, B., Eissen, S. M. Z., & Lipka, N. (2010). Web genre analysis: Use cases, retrieval models, and implementation issues Genres on the Web (pp. 167–189). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR95" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e493">2010</a>), as the information on the genre in a query in information retrieval tools would allow users to find the texts that are relevant for them more efficiently (Crowston et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Crowston, K., Kwaśnik, B., & Rubleske, J. (2010). Problems in the use-centered development of a taxonomy of web genres. Genres on the Web (pp. 69–84). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR18" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e496">2010</a>). Furthermore, collecting texts from the web has allowed a significantly faster and cheaper creation of corpora which are essential for language research and development of advanced language resources and technologies, especially in cases of under-resourced languages. However, in contrast to corpora that were carefully manually selected, web corpora are built in an automated way due to which their composition remains unknown (Baroni et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2009" title="Baroni, M., Bernardini, S., Ferraresi, A., & Zanchetta, E. (2009). The WaCky wide web: A collection of very large linguistically processed web-crawled corpora. Language Resources and Evaluation, 43(3), 209–226." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR8" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e499">2009</a>).</p><p>To obtain the information on the genre of specific texts in large collections of text, automatic genre identification (AGI), a text classification method which categorizes texts into genres, is the only feasible option due to the high data volume. AGI is primarily researched in the field of language technology which is concerned with computational processing of human languages and which encompasses computational linguistics and natural language processing (NLP), combining linguistics and computer science, especially artificial intelligence. As the authors of smaller, manually collected collections of texts are usually aware of the source of texts and their types, automatic genre identification is mostly studied to be applied on large web-based text collections where the source of texts is unknown. That is also why most of genre-annotated datasets surveyed in this paper contain texts from the web. However, since many high-coverage genre schemata, presented in this work, aim to cover all of the genre categories found in texts, the results of web genre identification research can be applied to collections of texts which do not originate from the web as well.</p><p>In addition to the benefits of genre identification for information retrieval and corpus creation and curation, it was shown that annotating documents with genre is also beneficial in many other NLP tasks. For instance, in part-of-speech (PoS) tagging of web corpora, Giesbrecht and Evert (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2009" title="Giesbrecht, E., & Evert, S. (2009). Is part-of-speech tagging a solved task? An evaluation of POS taggers for the German web as corpus. In: Proceedings of the Fifth Web as Corpus Workshop, pp. 27–35." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR32" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e508">2009</a>) showed that using different granularity of PoS sets depending on the genres improves the tagging accuracy. Stewart and Callan (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2009" title="Stewart, J. G., & Callan, J. (2009). Genre oriented summarization (Unpublished doctoral dissertation). Language Technologies Institute, School of Computer ScienceCarnegie Mellon University." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR96" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e511">2009</a>) showed that automatic genre identification improves automatic summarization, as the genre-oriented and goal-focused summarization algorithms outperformed other summarization methods. In addition to this, genres were revealed to be beneficial for machine translation (Van der Wees et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Van der Wees, M., Bisazza, A., & Monz, C. (2018). Evaluation of machine translation performance across multiple genres and languages. In: Proceedings of the Eleventh International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation (LREC 2018)." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR104" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e514">2018</a>) and zero-shot dependency parsing (Müller-Eberstein et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Müller-Eberstein, M., van der Goot, R., & Plank, B. (2021). Genre as Weak Supervision for Cross-lingual Dependency Parsing. In: Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pp. 4786–4802." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR68" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e517">2021</a>). Recently, genre has also been studied in the area of information security, where it can be used for automated genre-aware assessment of credibility of web documents (Agrawal et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2019" title="Agrawal, S., Sanagavarapu, L.M., & Reddy, Y.R. (2019). FACT-Fine grained assessment of web page CredibiliTy. In: TENCON 2019-2019 IEEE Region 10 Conference (TENCON), pp. 1088–1097." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR2" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e520">2019</a>).</p><p>Obtaining information on genres can be of great value in a wide range of disciplines, including linguistics, corpus linguistics, computational linguistics, natural language processing, information retrieval and information security. Therefore, automatic genre identification models would be a great resource, as manual annotation of thousands of texts with genre labels is expensive and time-consuming, and, despite the best efforts, it can often result in unreliable annotations. However, although various attempts have been made to provide schemata, genre-annotated datasets and classifiers, there are no reference datasets (Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S. (2010). In the garden and in the jungle genres on the web (pp. 149–166). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR88" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e527">2010</a>) that can be directly used for building an AGI classifier which could be applied to any collection of web documents. In previous work, researchers used various genre definitions, annotation practices and corpora collection methods, each of them having its advantages and disadvantages. Thus, when approaching the automatic genre identification (AGI) task, one must not only ponder the appropriate machine learning strategy, but needs to carefully define each step of the data collection, schema creation and data annotation process.</p><p>The objective of this paper is to present a detailed survey of the existing research on automatic genre identification and available genre datasets. The rest of the paper is organised as follows: Sect. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="section anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Sec2">2</a> presents various terms and definitions used to describe genres, which are the basis of genre schemata, discussed in Sect. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="section anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Sec3">3</a>. Section <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="section anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Sec4">4</a> compares existing genre-annotated datasets given the data collection methods and annotation approaches. The most frequently used datasets are presented in more detail. Section <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="section anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Sec11">5</a> presents an overview of text classification machine learning methods typically used for the automatic genre identification task, the results of various experiments, and the main challenges for automatic genre identification. Finally, Sect. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="section anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Sec12">6</a> concludes the paper by summarising its findings, and proposing directions for improvements in the area.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Genre definition"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec2-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec2"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">2 </span>Genre definition</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec2-content"><p>One of the main challenges of studying genre is that there is no consensus among researchers on the definition of the genre phenomenon, or how to differentiate between genres, what qualifies for a genre class, and, finally, what the optimal genre schema is. Even more, there is no consensus on the term used for this phenomenon. While many researchers use the term “genre” and describe this task as “automatic genre identification” (AGI) or “web genre identification” (WGI), others avoid this term and prefer derived analogues, such as “registers” (see Egbert et al. <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e556">2015</a> and further research by Laippala et al. <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2019" title="Laippala, V., Kyllönen, R., Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Pyysalo, S. (2019). Toward multilingual identification of online registers. In: Proceedings of the 22nd Nordic Conference on Computational Linguistics, pp. 292–297." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e559">2019</a>; Repo et al. <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Repo, L., Skantsi, V., Rönnqvist, S., Hellström, S., Oinonen, M., Salmela, A., & Laippala, V. (2021). Beyond the English web: Zero-shot cross-lingual and lightweight monolingual classification of registers. In: 16th Conference of the European Chapter of the Associationfor Computational Linguistics: Student Research Workshop, EACL 2021, pp. 183–191." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR77" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e562">2021</a>; Ronnqvist et al. <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Rönnqvist, S., Skantsi, V., Oinonen, M., & Laippala, V. (2021). Multilingual and zero-shot is closing in on monolingual web register classification. In: Proceedings of the 23rd Nordic Conference on Computational Linguistics (NoDaLiDa), pp. 157–165." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR80" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e565">2021</a>), “functional text dimensions” (see Sharoff <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Sharoff, S. (2018). Functional text dimensions for the annotation of web corpora. Corpora, 13(1), 65–95." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR89" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e568">2018</a>) or “text types” (see Stubbs <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1996" title="Stubbs, M. (1996). Text and corpus analysis: Computer-assisted studies of language and culture. Blackwell Oxford." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR99" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e572">1996</a>). While extensive work has been dedicated to navigate this “terminological maze”, as Moessner (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2001" title="Moessner, L. (2001). Genre, text type, style, register: A terminological maze? European Journal of English Studies, 5(2), 131–138." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR67" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e575">2001</a>) put it, especially to distinguish between registers and genres (see Biber and Conrad <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2019" title="Biber, D., & Conrad, S. (2019). Register, genre, and style. Cambridge University Press." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR10" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e578">2019</a>, Sharoff <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Sharoff, S. (2021). Genre annotation for the web: text-external and textinternal perspectives. Register studies." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR87" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e581">2021</a>, Lee <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2002A" title="Lee, D. (2002). Genres, registers, text types, domains and styles: Clarifying the concepts and navigating a path through the BNC jungle. Teaching and learning by doing corpus analysis (pp. 245–292). Brill Rodopi." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR58" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e584">2002A</a>), some researchers use the two terms interchangeably and argue that the distinction between them is “not relevant, and the choice between genre and register comes down to personal preference or tradition” (Egbert et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e587">2015</a>). However, in linguistics and especially sociolinguistics the term “register” is used to describe a different aspect of language variation, connected with conversational context. Frequent register categories are “academic language”, “non-standard language”, “formal language” and so on (see Lukin et al. <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2011" title="Lukin, A., Moore, A.R., Herke, M., Wegener, R., & Wu, C. (2011). Halliday’s model of register revisited and explored." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR63" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e591">2011</a>). According to Lee (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2002A" title="Lee, D. (2002). Genres, registers, text types, domains and styles: Clarifying the concepts and navigating a path through the BNC jungle. Teaching and learning by doing corpus analysis (pp. 245–292). Brill Rodopi." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR58" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e594">2002A</a>), the largest difference between the concepts of genres and registers is that genres describe whole texts, while registers are defined based on internal linguistic patterns, which are independent of text-level structures.</p><p>In addition to this, another challenge is how to define genres, an endeavour described by Chandler (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1997" title="Chandler, D. (1997). An introduction to genre theory." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR15" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e600">1997</a>) as a “theoretical minefield". In general, most definitions describe genre classes based on the socially recognized form of a document and its intended communicative purpose (Kwasnik & Crowston, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2005" title="Kwaśnik, B. H., & Crowston, K. (2005). Introduction to the special issue: Genres of digital documents. Information Technology & People." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR49" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e603">2005</a>). In addition to this, some definitions also consider the target audience (Eissen & Stein, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Zu Eissen, S.M., & Stein, B. (2004). Genre classification of web pages. In: Annual Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 256–269." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR109" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e606">2004</a>), expectations of the reader (Santini, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2006" title="Santini, S.M. (2006). Common criteria for genre classification: Annotation and granularity. In: Workshop on Text-based Information Retrieval (TIR-06). Conjunction with ECAI 2006, Riva del Garda, 2006." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR83" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e609">2006</a>), style (Finn & Kushmerick, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2006" title="Finn, A., & Kushmerick, N. (2006). Learning to classify documents according to genre. Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 57(11), 1506–1518." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR27" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e612">2006</a>; Argamon et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1998" title="Argamon, S., Koppel, M., & Avneri, G. (1998). Routing documents according to style. In: First International Workshop on Innovative Information Systems, pp. 85–92." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR3" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e616">1998</a>), or the content of the texts (Rosso, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2008" title="Rosso, M. A. (2008). User-based identification of Web genres. Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 59(7), 1053–1072." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR81" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e619">2008</a>). To identify genres, researchers observe their intrinsic features, i.e., the linguistic and other “look’n’feel” features in the text (text-internal perspective), their extrinsic features, that is the function of the texts (text-external or functional perspective), or both (see Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S. (2010). In the garden and in the jungle genres on the web (pp. 149–166). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR88" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e622">2010</a>, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Sharoff, S. (2021). Genre annotation for the web: text-external and textinternal perspectives. Register studies." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR87" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e625">2021</a>) for a detailed discussion on both perspectives).</p><p>Moreover, studying genres, especially genres of digital texts, is a “formidable undertaking”, to cite Kwasnik and Crowston (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2005" title="Kwaśnik, B. H., & Crowston, K. (2005). Introduction to the special issue: Genres of digital documents. Information Technology & People." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR49" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e631">2005</a>), due to fundamental difficulties connected with the genre notion itself. Firstly, conventional characteristics of a genre category can change over time and instances can be more or less prototypical in a specific time period (see Santini et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Santini, M., Mehler, A., & Sharoff, S. (2010). Riding the rough waves of genre on the web. Genres on the Web (pp. 3–30). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR86" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e634">2010</a>), Santini (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2006" title="Santini, S.M. (2006). Common criteria for genre classification: Annotation and granularity. In: Workshop on Text-based Information Retrieval (TIR-06). Conjunction with ECAI 2006, Riva del Garda, 2006." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR83" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e637">2006</a>)). The evolution of genres was especially notable after the introduction of the World Wide Web, when researchers observed emergence of new genres, unique to the web, and existing genres that evolved to adapt to the new medium (Williams & Crowston, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2000" title="Williams, M., & Crowston, Kevin. (2000). Reproduced and emergent genres of communication on the World WideWeb. Information Society, 16(3), 201–215." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR106" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e640">2000</a>). Although many genres of web documents exist also in traditional texts, genres on the web are less fixed (Kwasnik & Crowston, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2005" title="Kwaśnik, B. H., & Crowston, K. (2005). Introduction to the special issue: Genres of digital documents. Information Technology & People." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR49" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e643">2005</a>). Secondly, some web documents can be hybrids, which means that a single text can display characteristics of multiple genres, e.g., an advertorial, a document that has the form of a news article, but the purpose of a promotion of a product (see Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Sharoff, S. (2021). Genre annotation for the web: text-external and textinternal perspectives. Register studies." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR87" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e647">2021</a>) and Repo et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Repo, L., Skantsi, V., Rönnqvist, S., Hellström, S., Oinonen, M., Salmela, A., & Laippala, V. (2021). Beyond the English web: Zero-shot cross-lingual and lightweight monolingual classification of registers. In: 16th Conference of the European Chapter of the Associationfor Computational Linguistics: Student Research Workshop, EACL 2021, pp. 183–191." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR77" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e650">2021</a>)). Thirdly, some web documents might not have any discernible characteristics of a genre class. They can be too short to reveal the purpose of the communication. They can also be of an emerging genre, or a specialized genre with which the reader is not familiar with, e.g., a shipping invoice, used by accountants (see Williams and Crowston (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2000" title="Williams, M., & Crowston, Kevin. (2000). Reproduced and emergent genres of communication on the World WideWeb. Information Society, 16(3), 201–215." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR106" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e653">2000</a>)). In addition to this, it is argued that genre can only be realized in a complete text (Biber & Conrad, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2019" title="Biber, D., & Conrad, S. (2019). Register, genre, and style. Cambridge University Press." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR10" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e656">2019</a>), which is not always available after the extraction of the text from a web page, a process that often includes removal of boilerplate content and other imperfect processing methods (see Pomikálek (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2011" title="Pomikálek, J. (2011). Removing boilerplate and duplicate content from web corpora (Unpublished doctoral dissertation). Masaryk university Faculty of informatics." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR72" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e659">2011</a>)).</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Genre schemata"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec3-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec3"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">3 </span>Genre schemata</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec3-content"><p>Eissen and Stein (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Zu Eissen, S.M., & Stein, B. (2004). Genre classification of web pages. In: Annual Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 256–269." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR109" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e670">2004</a>) noted that an “inherent problem of web genre classification is that even humans are not able to consistently specify the genre of a given page”. Text instances can be more or less prototypical examples of its genre classes, can be hybrids or can lack characteristics of any genre. Thus, it is crucial for the reliability of a genre-annotated dataset that the genre schema supports the annotators so that their decisions are as consistent as possible. As no reference schema exists, most studies use their own, devised in accordance with the aim of the research. Schemata, used in previous work, vary significantly in terms of the number of classes, which range from seven (Santini, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Santini, M. (2007). Automatic identification of genre in web pages (Unpublished doctoral dissertation). University of Brighton." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR84" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e673">2007</a>; Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S. (2010). In the garden and in the jungle genres on the web (pp. 149–166). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR88" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e676">2010</a>; Lee & Myaeng, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2002b" title="Lee, Y.-B., & Myaeng, S.H. (2002). Text genre classification with genrerevealing and subject-revealing features. In: Proceedings of the 25th Annual International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval, pp. 145–150." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR56" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e679">2002b</a>) to more than a hundred (Roussinov et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2001" title="Roussinov, D., Crowston, K., Nilan, M., Kwasnik, B., Cai, J., & Liu, X. (2001). Genre based navigation on the web. In: Proceedings of the 34th annual Hawaii international conference on system sciences, p. 10." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR82" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e682">2001</a>) or almost 300 classes (Crowston et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Crowston, K., Kwaśnik, B., & Rubleske, J. (2010). Problems in the use-centered development of a taxonomy of web genres. Genres on the Web (pp. 69–84). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR18" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e686">2010</a>). They are either hierarchical (Stubbe & Ringlstetter, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Stubbe, A., & Ringlstetter, C. (2007). Recognizing genres. Towards a reference corpus of web genres: Proceedings." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR98" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e689">2007</a>; Egbert et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e692">2015</a>) or not (Asheghi et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e695">2016</a>; Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Sharoff, S. (2018). Functional text dimensions for the annotation of web corpora. Corpora, 13(1), 65–95." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR89" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e698">2018</a>).</p><p>Most existing schemata consist of around 10 to 20 categories, while some of them comprise of more than 50 genre classes (see Crowston et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Crowston, K., Kwaśnik, B., & Rubleske, J. (2010). Problems in the use-centered development of a taxonomy of web genres. Genres on the Web (pp. 69–84). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR18" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e704">2010</a>); Roussinov et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2001" title="Roussinov, D., Crowston, K., Nilan, M., Kwasnik, B., Cai, J., & Liu, X. (2001). Genre based navigation on the web. In: Proceedings of the 34th annual Hawaii international conference on system sciences, p. 10." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR82" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e707">2001</a>); Williams and Crowston (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2000" title="Williams, M., & Crowston, Kevin. (2000). Reproduced and emergent genres of communication on the World WideWeb. Information Society, 16(3), 201–215." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR106" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e710">2000</a>); Egbert et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e713">2015</a>); Berninger et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2008" title="Berninger, V.F., Kim, Y., & Ross, S. (2008). Building a document genre corpus: a profile of the KRYS I corpus. BCS-IRSG Workshop on Corpus Profiling, pp. 1–10." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR9" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e716">2008</a>)). Larger granularity usually increases the annotation complexity which results in a lower inter-annotator agreement and a less reliable dataset (see Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S. (2010). In the garden and in the jungle genres on the web (pp. 149–166). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR88" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e720">2010</a>)). However, it should be noted that although a smaller set results in broader categories, they should still be limited by functional and form constraints so that the texts belonging to them share certain distinguishing properties, as argued by Asheghi et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e723">2016</a>). As in the case of a high granularity, too broad categories can also negatively impact the reliability of the annotated dataset and can be less useful for automatic identification. In addition to this, if the aim of a genre schema is to capture the entire diversity of genres on the web, Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Sharoff, S. (2021). Genre annotation for the web: text-external and textinternal perspectives. Register studies." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR87" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e726">2021</a>) warned that genres are not fixed and writers are not constrained to following genre norms, thus, one should be aware that there will always exist web documents which do not fit under any genre class. While most studies used a pre-defined closed set of labels, some previous work took this issue into consideration, i.e., Asheghi et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e729">2016</a>) and Kuzman et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2022b" title="Kuzman, T., Rupnik, P., & Ljubešić, N. (2022). The GINCO training dataset for web genre identification of documents out in the wild. Proceedings of the language resources and evaluation conference (pp. 1584–1594). European Language Resources Association." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR47" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e732">2022b</a>) included a category <i>Other</i> in the schema, and Pritsos and Stamatatos (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Pritsos, D., & Stamatatos, E. (2018). Open set evaluation of web genre identification. Language Resources and Evaluation, 52(4), 949–968." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR73" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e739">2018</a>) used an open-set classification approach, allowing for a document not to be associated with any genre class.</p><p>Most of the schemata were developed following the top-down approach, which is based on theoretical principles, researchers’ knowledge and understanding of the domain, and categorization from previous research. In regard to this approach, Rehm et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2008" title="Rehm, G., Santini, M., Mehler, A., Braslavski, P., Gleim, R., Stubbe, A., & Vidulin, V. (2008). Towards a reference corpus of web genres for the evaluation of genre identification systems. Lrec." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR76" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e745">2008</a>) proposed that the researchers should take advantage of accumulated expert knowledge, to avoid choosing the genre set based solely on how they perceive the classes, because the end users without a linguistic education might understand genre categories differently than genre researchers. By deriving the schema from category sets proposed by various research groups, this approach leads to an improved set of categories that have already been proven to be applicable to the variety of language in actual document collections. An alternative approach is the bottom-up approach, taken up by some researchers (Crowston et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Crowston, K., Kwaśnik, B., & Rubleske, J. (2010). Problems in the use-centered development of a taxonomy of web genres. Genres on the Web (pp. 69–84). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR18" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e748">2010</a>; Dewe et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1998" title="Dewe, J., Karlgren, J., & Bretan, I. (1998). Assembling a balanced corpus from the internet. In: Proceedings of the 11th Nordic Conference of Computational Linguistics (NODALIDA 1998), pp. 100–108." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR23" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e751">1998</a>; Eissen & Stein, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Zu Eissen, S.M., & Stein, B. (2004). Genre classification of web pages. In: Annual Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 256–269." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR109" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e754">2004</a>; Egbert et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e757">2015</a>), which is based on surveys of web users. This approach revealed to be problematic as the respondents were not consistent, they had difficulties with naming genres or used general or unspecific terms (see Crowston et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Crowston, K., Kwaśnik, B., & Rubleske, J. (2010). Problems in the use-centered development of a taxonomy of web genres. Genres on the Web (pp. 69–84). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR18" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e761">2010</a>)).</p><p>The main factor defining the composition of genre schemata in previous works was the aim with which the genre dataset was constructed. Some researchers aimed to create a schema which would cover all possible genre variation found in (mostly web) texts. Such datasets allow for creation of general-purpose classifiers which would be able to classify any text into some genre class. In contrast, other researchers were not interested in covering all of the diversity found in text collections. They rather focused on a smaller set of specific genres that they deemed to be the most useful for search engine users who would find texts more efficiently based on genre criteria. In addition, some other schemata and corresponding genre datasets were developed with the aim to study characteristics of specific genres, such as poetry and prose, or with the aim of improving manual annotation. Thus, based on the aim of genre research, we divided the genre schemata into the following groups: </p><ol class="u-list-style-none">
                <li>
                  <span class="u-custom-list-number">1.</span>
                  
                    <p>High-coverage schemata (complete genre taxonomy) which aim to cover the entire genre composition of the web. These studies mostly used larger sets of specific classes (see Stubbe and Ringlstetter (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Stubbe, A., & Ringlstetter, C. (2007). Recognizing genres. Towards a reference corpus of web genres: Proceedings." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR98" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e777">2007</a>); Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Sharoff, S. (2018). Functional text dimensions for the annotation of web corpora. Corpora, 13(1), 65–95." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR89" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e780">2018</a>); Egbert et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e783">2015</a>); Laippala et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2019" title="Laippala, V., Kyllönen, R., Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Pyysalo, S. (2019). Toward multilingual identification of online registers. In: Proceedings of the 22nd Nordic Conference on Computational Linguistics, pp. 292–297." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e786">2019</a>); Kuzman et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2022b" title="Kuzman, T., Rupnik, P., & Ljubešić, N. (2022). The GINCO training dataset for web genre identification of documents out in the wild. Proceedings of the language resources and evaluation conference (pp. 1584–1594). European Language Resources Association." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR47" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e789">2022b</a>); Suchomel (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2020" title="Suchomel, V. (2020). Genre Annotation of Web Corpora: Scheme and Issues. In: Proceedings of the Future Technologies Conference, pp. 738–754." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR101" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e793">2020</a>)), a smaller set of broader categories (see Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S. (2010). In the garden and in the jungle genres on the web (pp. 149–166). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR88" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e796">2010</a>)) or a combination of the two (see Santini (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Santini, M. (2010). Cross-testing a genre classification model for the web. Genres on the Web (pp. 87–128). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR85" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e799">2010</a>)).</p>
                  
                </li>
                <li>
                  <span class="u-custom-list-number">2.</span>
                  
                    <p>Information retrieval schemata, created with the aim to provide genre identification inside the search engines. Thus, they consist of genre categories that are deemed to be useful for the search engine users (see Eissen and Stein (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Zu Eissen, S.M., & Stein, B. (2004). Genre classification of web pages. In: Annual Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 256–269." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR109" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e813">2004</a>); Vidulin et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Vidulin, V., Luštrek, M., & Gams, M. (2007). Using genres to improve search engines. In: 1st International Workshop: Towards Genre-Enabled Search Engines: The Impact of Natural Language Processing, pp. 45–51." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR105" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e816">2007</a>); Roussinov et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2001" title="Roussinov, D., Crowston, K., Nilan, M., Kwasnik, B., Cai, J., & Liu, X. (2001). Genre based navigation on the web. In: Proceedings of the 34th annual Hawaii international conference on system sciences, p. 10." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR82" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e819">2001</a>); Dewe et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1998" title="Dewe, J., Karlgren, J., & Bretan, I. (1998). Assembling a balanced corpus from the internet. In: Proceedings of the 11th Nordic Conference of Computational Linguistics (NODALIDA 1998), pp. 100–108." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR23" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e822">1998</a>); Lim et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2005" title="Lim, C. S., Lee, K. J., & Kim, G. C. (2005). Multiple sets of features for automatic genre classification of web documents. Information Processing and Management, 41(5), 1263–1276." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR62" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e825">2005</a>); Santini (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Santini, M. (2007). Automatic identification of genre in web pages (Unpublished doctoral dissertation). University of Brighton." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR84" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e829">2007</a>)).</p>
                  
                </li>
                <li>
                  <span class="u-custom-list-number">3.</span>
                  
                    <p>Schemata, developed with other aims: limited sets of categories used in studies which analyse one or a few genre classes, e.g., a smaller set of genres of interest ( Boese (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2005" title="Boese, E.S. (2005). Stereotyping the web: Genre classification of web documents (Unpublished doctoral dissertation). Citeseer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR13" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e843">2005</a>); Lee and Myaeng (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Lee, Y.-B., & Myaeng, S.H. (2004). Automatic identification of text genres and their roles in subject-based categorization. In: 37th Annual Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR57" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e846">2004</a>); Asheghi et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e849">2016</a>)), academic genres (Rehm, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2002" title="Rehm, G. (2002). Towards automatic Web genre identification: a corpus-based approach in the domain of academia by example of the Academic’s Personal Homepage. In: Proceedings of the 35th Annual Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences, pp. 1143–1152." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR75" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e852">2002</a>), e-shop genres (Levering et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2008" title="Levering, R., Cutler, M., & Yu, L. (2008). Using visual features for fine-grained genre classification of web pages. The reality in the underlying datasets is much more complicated. Labels that have same or similar names do not necessarily cover similar texts, as this depends on the researchers’ and annotators’ understanding of the labels. Moreover, the texts inside similarly named classes in different datasets could differ significantly also based on the approaches, with which the datasets were collected, as described in the following section.</p><p>The case of journalistic genres illustrates well the differences between the schemata and shows why it is infeasible to merge any datasets, even if their labels have similar names. For instance, the Genre-KI-04 dataset (Eissen & Stein, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Zu Eissen, S.M., & Stein, B. (2004). Genre classification of web pages. In: Annual Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 256–269." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR109" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1307">2004</a>) includes a label <i>Article</i>, for which one might assume that it represents news articles. However, in the documentation accompanying the dataset, the label is defined as “Documents with longer passages of text, such as research articles, reviews, technical reports, or book chapters”. The label thus includes a large variety of texts, including opinionated texts, such as the instance in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Fig1">1</a>. In the 20-Genre Collection (MGC) (Vidulin et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Vidulin, V., Luštrek, M., & Gams, M. (2007). Using genres to improve search engines. In: 1st International Workshop: Towards Genre-Enabled Search Engines: The Impact of Natural Language Processing, pp. 45–51." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR105" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1316">2007</a>), a genre that could be connected to news articles based on the name is <i>Journalistic</i>. Its definition further confirms this: “conveys mostly objective information on current events” (Vidulin et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Vidulin, V., Luštrek, M., & Gams, M. (2007). Using genres to improve search engines. In: 1st International Workshop: Towards Genre-Enabled Search Engines: The Impact of Natural Language Processing, pp. 45–51." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR105" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1323">2007</a>). However, on their website,<sup><a href="#Fn1"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>1</a></sup> authors included the following types of texts under the <i>Journalistic</i> genre: news, reportages, editorials, interviews and reviews, indicating that the class is quite broad and includes objective as well as subjective texts. The great inner variation between the texts, included in this genre, can be seen in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Fig2">2</a>. In the CORE dataset (Egbert et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1344">2015</a>), the news article genre is divided into two categories – <i>News Report/Blog</i> and <i>Sports Report</i> – based on the topic of articles. In addition, the schema also includes a class, named <i>Magazine Article</i>. The <i>News Report/Blog</i> genre is defined in the annotation guidelines<sup><a href="#Fn2"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>2</a></sup> as a “news report written by journalists and published by news outlets” with the purpose to report on recent events.
