They are the basis for training machine learning models for automatic genre identification. Some genre researchers used traditional general-purpose corpora that have genre information, such as Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA) (Davies, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2008" title="Davies, M. (2008). The Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA). Available online at 
                  https://www.english-corpora.org/ coca/
                  
                " href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR20" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1458">2008</a>) (see Ströbel et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Ströbel, M., Kerz, E., Wiechmann, D., & Qiao, Y. (2018). Text genre classification based on linguistic complexity contours using a recurrent neural network. MRC@ IJCAI, pp. 56–63." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR97" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1461">2018</a>)), British National Corpus (BNC) (Lee, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2002A" title="Lee, D. (2002). Genres, registers, text types, domains and styles: Clarifying the concepts and navigating a path through the BNC jungle. Teaching and learning by doing corpus analysis (pp. 245–292). Brill Rodopi." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR58" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1464">2002A</a>) (see Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S. (2010). In the garden and in the jungle genres on the web (pp. 149–166). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR88" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1467">2010</a>)) and Brown Corpus (Kučera & Francis, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1967" title="Kučera, H., & Francis, W. N. (1967). Computational analysis of present-day American English. Brown University Press." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR44" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1470">1967</a>) (see Karlgren and Cutting (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1994" title="Karlgren, J., & Cutting, D. (1994). Recognizing text genres with simple metrics using discriminant analysis. In: Proceedings of the 15th International Conference on Computational Linguistics." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR39" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1474">1994</a>)). However, these datasets do not represent well the challenges for automatic genre identification imposed by less curated web text collections, where there is much wider variation between styles and quality of texts (Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S. (2010). In the garden and in the jungle genres on the web (pp. 149–166). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR88" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1477">2010</a>). That is why in the great majority of studies, the genre researchers decided to construct their own datasets based on web data. The process of building genre-annotated datasets regularly starts with a selection of data to be manually annotated, as described in Sect. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="section anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Sec5">4.1</a>. Next, manual annotation for genre is performed, as discussed in Sect. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="section anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Sec6">4.2</a>. We wrap up this section with an overview of various types of manually annotated datasets in Sect. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="section anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Sec7">4.3</a>.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec5"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">4.1 </span>Data Selection</h3><p>Most datasets that are manually annotated for genre consist of texts originating from the web. The texts are either taken from existing web corpora, or new document collections are constructed in a manual or an automated manner.</p><p>As genre-annotated datasets were created with different aims, and financial and technical constraints, they largely differ in terms of size, collection methods and document format. In many studies, the datasets were limited to document formats which are easier to obtain from the web and to process with automated methods, such as HTML. This influences the genre distribution in the final dataset, as by not including PDF files or Word documents, certain genres for which the preferred format is PDF, such as research papers and catalogues, are likely under-represented (Santini et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Santini, M., Mehler, A., & Sharoff, S. (2010). Riding the rough waves of genre on the web. Genres on the Web (pp. 3–30). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR86" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1499">2010</a>).</p><p>Based on the collection method, web corpora can be categorized into designed and crawled corpora (Kilgarriff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2012" title="Kilgarriff, A. (2012). Getting to know your corpus. In: International Conference on Text, Speech and Dialogue, pp. 3–15." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR42" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1505">2012</a>). In designed corpora, texts are collected based on certain criteria, defined by the researchers. Although this collection method facilitates the annotation and machine classification, Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S. (2010). In the garden and in the jungle genres on the web (pp. 149–166). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR88" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1508">2010</a>) argues that designed corpora are not representative of the actual genre distribution on the web. They are thus less useful for training a genre classifier that would be applied on a new text collection. In contrast, crawled corpora represent a “(more or less faithful) snapshot of the web” (Asheghi et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1511">2016</a>). Examples of designed corpora are those by Stubbe and Ringlstetter (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Stubbe, A., & Ringlstetter, C. (2007). Recognizing genres. Towards a reference corpus of web genres: Proceedings." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR98" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1514">2007</a>), Santini (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Santini, M. (2007). Automatic identification of genre in web pages (Unpublished doctoral dissertation). University of Brighton." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR84" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1517">2007</a>), Boese (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2005" title="Boese, E.S. (2005). Stereotyping the web: Genre classification of web documents (Unpublished doctoral dissertation). Citeseer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR13" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1521">2005</a>), Berninger et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2008" title="Berninger, V.F., Kim, Y., & Ross, S. (2008). Building a document genre corpus: a profile of the KRYS I corpus. BCS-IRSG Workshop on Corpus Profiling, pp. 1–10." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR9" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1524">2008</a>), while Laippala et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2020" title="Laippala, V., Rönnqvist, S., Hellström, S., Luotolahti, J., Repo, L., Salmela, A., & Pyysalo, S. (2020). From web crawl to clean register-annotated corpora. In: Proceedings of the 12th Web as Corpus Workshop, pp. 14–22." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR52" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1527">2020</a>), Kuzman et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2022b" title="Kuzman, T., Rupnik, P., & Ljubešić, N. (2022). The GINCO training dataset for web genre identification of documents out in the wild. Proceedings of the language resources and evaluation conference (pp. 1584–1594). European Language Resources Association." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR47" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1530">2022b</a>) and Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Sharoff, S. (2018). Functional text dimensions for the annotation of web corpora. Corpora, 13(1), 65–95." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR89" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1533">2018</a>) used samples of crawled corpora. Rehm et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2008" title="Rehm, G., Santini, M., Mehler, A., Braslavski, P., Gleim, R., Stubbe, A., & Vidulin, V. (2008). Towards a reference corpus of web genres for the evaluation of genre identification systems. Lrec." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR76" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1536">2008</a>) proposed using both methods, which was done by Asheghi et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1540">2016</a>). They first collected a designed corpus consisting of prototypical instances to test their method of manual annotation, and then extended their research to a random collection of web texts to analyse the coverage of the genre schema and the reliability of annotation in a more realistic setting. Another commonly used method for data collection is retrieving top hits of automated queries made to a search engine (see Egbert et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1543">2015</a>); Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S. (2010). In the garden and in the jungle genres on the web (pp. 149–166). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR88" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1546">2010</a>); Lim et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2005" title="Lim, C. S., Lee, K. J., & Kim, G. C. (2005). Multiple sets of features for automatic genre classification of web documents. Information Processing and Management, 41(5), 1263–1276." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR62" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1549">2005</a>)). However, one should be aware that the final composition of such collection might be impacted by the choice of keywords in the queries and by the searching and ranking algorithms used by the search engines which favour more popular pages (see Santini et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Santini, M., Mehler, A., & Sharoff, S. (2010). Riding the rough waves of genre on the web. Genres on the Web (pp. 3–30). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR86" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1552">2010</a>); Asheghi et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1555">2016</a>)). This can result in a bias towards certain genres, such as e-shops. Furthermore, this method allows collecting only documents that can be found on the searchable web (Egbert et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1559">2015</a>).</p><p>Being aware of the impact of the collection method on the resulting dataset, Asheghi et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1565">2016</a>) and Lim et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2005" title="Lim, C. S., Lee, K. J., & Kim, G. C. (2005). Multiple sets of features for automatic genre classification of web documents. Information Processing and Management, 41(5), 1263–1276." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR62" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1568">2005</a>) devoted attention to assuring that the texts from the crawled corpus originate from a wide variety of sources, to avoid biases towards certain topics, authors or sources, thereby guaranteeing generalizability of the resulting datasets. Furthermore, Asheghi et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1571">2016</a>) and Kuzman et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2022b" title="Kuzman, T., Rupnik, P., & Ljubešić, N. (2022). The GINCO training dataset for web genre identification of documents out in the wild. Proceedings of the language resources and evaluation conference (pp. 1584–1594). European Language Resources Association." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR47" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1574">2022b</a>) assured temporal diversity of sources, by selecting sources published at several time points, as some genres, such as <i>News</i>, have strong temporal connection to topics.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec6"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">4.2 </span>Annotation practices</h3><p>In addition to the corpus collection methods that the datasets are based on, one of the most crucial factors for producing a high-quality dataset that can be used for machine learning experiments is reliable manual annotation. The annotation can be performed by a smaller group of experts, such as in the case of Santini (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2006" title="Santini, S.M. (2006). Common criteria for genre classification: Annotation and granularity. In: Workshop on Text-based Information Retrieval (TIR-06). Conjunction with ECAI 2006, Riva del Garda, 2006." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR83" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1588">2006</a>); Vidulin et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Vidulin, V., Luštrek, M., & Gams, M. (2007). Using genres to improve search engines. In: 1st International Workshop: Towards Genre-Enabled Search Engines: The Impact of Natural Language Processing, pp. 45–51." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR105" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1591">2007</a>); Eissen and Stein (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Zu Eissen, S.M., & Stein, B. (2004). Genre classification of web pages. In: Annual Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 256–269." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR109" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1594">2004</a>). However, as the task is very time-consuming, annotation campaigns in previous research mostly resulted in relatively small datasets, consisting of less than 2,000 texts. To achieve faster and cheaper manual annotation, some researchers leveraged the advent of crowd-sourcing. This is how two of the biggest English genre-annotated corpora were created, the Leeds Web Genre Corpus (Asheghi et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1597">2016</a>) and the CORE corpus (Egbert et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1600">2015</a>). The decision to opt for crowd-sourcing was based on the previous findings (see Snow et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2008" title="Snow, R., O’connor, B., Jurafsky, D., & Ng, A.Y. (2008). Cheap and fast– but is it good? Evaluating non-expert annotations for natural language tasks. In: Proceedings of the 2008 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pp. 254–263." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR93" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1604">2008</a>)) which compared expert and crowd-sourcing annotation on various tasks and concluded that if four non-experts annotate the same instance, the final annotations are often comparable to the expert-annotation quality. In addition to this, Asheghi et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1607">2016</a>) argue that this is the most appropriate annotation method, because it avoids potential bias from the experts who both developed the genre schema and annotated the dataset.</p><p>Furthermore, annotation strategies vary based on how researchers dealt with hybridity of web texts. As mentioned in the Introduction, classifying web texts in genre categories can be challenging, because some texts, known as hybrid texts, can have characteristics of multiple genres. The hybridity of texts might be intentional, which is the case of an advertorial – a promotion of a product written in a form of a news article to appear more trustworthy to the readers. It might also occur due to authors’ lack of expertise or willingness to follow traditionally accepted genre characteristics (Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Sharoff, S. (2021). Genre annotation for the web: text-external and textinternal perspectives. Register studies." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR87" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1613">2021</a>). In contrast to non-digital texts which are often reviewed before being printed and published, a much larger number of texts on the web does not undergo any editorial control which would compel the authors to follow genre norms.</p><p>In addition to hybrid texts where characteristics of multiple genres are intertwined, there exist multi-class documents, which consist of a selection of functionally-separated texts of different genres that were published on the same web page and thus belong to a single document (Stubbe & Ringlstetter, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Stubbe, A., & Ringlstetter, C. (2007). Recognizing genres. Towards a reference corpus of web genres: Proceedings." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR98" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1619">2007</a>). An example of a multi-class document is a document from a web page consisting of a news article, followed by the readers’ comments. A special and the most-challenging case of multi-class documents are documents where text in another genre is embedded in another text (see Williams and Crowston (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2000" title="Williams, M., & Crowston, Kevin. (2000). Reproduced and emergent genres of communication on the World WideWeb. Information Society, 16(3), 201–215." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR106" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1622">2000</a>)), such as a blog post that includes an entire letter. To assure a reliable annotation, challenges with hybrid texts and multi-class documents need to be addressed in the data selection and annotation procedure. Some previous studies tackled the issue with hybrid texts by allowing multi-label annotation, i.e., assigning multiple labels to a single text (Vidulin et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Vidulin, V., Luštrek, M., & Gams, M. (2007). Using genres to improve search engines. In: 1st International Workshop: Towards Genre-Enabled Search Engines: The Impact of Natural Language Processing, pp. 45–51." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR105" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1625">2007</a>; Laippala et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2019" title="Laippala, V., Kyllönen, R., Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Pyysalo, S. (2019). Toward multilingual identification of online registers. In: Proceedings of the 22nd Nordic Conference on Computational Linguistics, pp. 292–297." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1628">2019</a>; Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Sharoff, S. (2018). Functional text dimensions for the annotation of web corpora. Corpora, 13(1), 65–95." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR89" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1631">2018</a>; Suchomel, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2020" title="Suchomel, V. (2020). Genre Annotation of Web Corpora: Scheme and Issues. In: Proceedings of the Future Technologies Conference, pp. 738–754." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR101" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1635">2020</a>; Egbert et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1638">2015</a>; Kuzman et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2022b" title="Kuzman, T., Rupnik, P., & Ljubešić, N. (2022). The GINCO training dataset for web genre identification of documents out in the wild. Proceedings of the language resources and evaluation conference (pp. 1584–1594). European Language Resources Association." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR47" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1641">2022b</a>).</p><p>The reliability of the annotation procedure is commonly evaluated based on the inter-annotator agreement, i.e., agreement of two or more annotators on the label of the same instance. That is why most of the datasets were annotated by at least 2 annotators. However, their reliability cannot be directly compared, because different methods were used to calculate the agreement: percentage agreement (in Asheghi et al. For instance, Suchomel (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2020" title="Suchomel, V. (2020). Genre Annotation of Web Corpora: Scheme and Issues. In: Proceedings of the Future Technologies Conference, pp. 738–754." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR101" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1704">2020</a>) concluded that a high agreement in this task is “hardly possible”. This is also the case for two of the datasets that have been recently most frequently used, the Corpus of Online Registers of English (CORE) (Egbert et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1707">2015</a>) and the Functional Text Dimensions (FTD) dataset (Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Sharoff, S. (2018). Functional text dimensions for the annotation of web corpora. Corpora, 13(1), 65–95." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR89" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1710">2018</a>). For CORE (Egbert et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1713">2015</a>), an analysis of the inter-annotator agreement revealed that there was no majority agreement, i.e., agreement between at least three of four annotators, on one-third of texts on the level of 8 main categories, and on half of the texts on the level of 53 subcategories. When Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Sharoff, S. (2018). Functional text dimensions for the annotation of web corpora. Corpora, 13(1), 65–95." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR89" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1716">2018</a>) applied the CORE schema and annotation process on another dataset, the inter-annotator agreement reached a nominal Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.66 and 0.53 for main categories and subcategories respectively, which is on the verge and below the acceptable threshold of 0.67, defined by Krippendorff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Krippendorff, K. (2018). Content analysis: An introduction to its methodology. Sage publications." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR43" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1720">2018</a>). For the FTD dataset, the inter-annotator agreement initially revealed encouraging results, reaching Krippendorff’s alpha above 0.76 (Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Sharoff, S. (2018). Functional text dimensions for the annotation of web corpora. Corpora, 13(1), 65–95." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR89" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1723">2018</a>). However, when the annotation was extended to another dataset in subsequent research by Suchomel (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2020" title="Suchomel, V. (2020). Genre Annotation of Web Corpora: Scheme and Issues. In: Proceedings of the Future Technologies Conference, pp. 738–754." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR101" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1726">2020</a>), the minimal acceptable Krippendorff’s alpha was not reached despite using a smaller set of labels. Recently, based on the findings from the previously discussed work, Kuzman et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2022b" title="Kuzman, T., Rupnik, P., & Ljubešić, N. (2022). The GINCO training dataset for web genre identification of documents out in the wild. Proceedings of the language resources and evaluation conference (pp. 1584–1594). European Language Resources Association." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR47" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1729">2022b</a>) considered assuring a reliable annotation at every step of their research. They devised their genre schema based on the categories from previous schemata so that the categories would be widely used and the label names would be recognizable to the annotators. The authors also opted for expert annotators instead of crowd-sourcing, and devised a decision tree survey and detailed guidelines with examples which led the annotators through their decision process. The results of the annotation campaign showed that this endeavour resulted in an inter-annotator agreement up to the nominal Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.71.</p><p>To avoid time-consuming and costly manual annotation, Santini (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2006" title="Santini, S.M. (2006). Common criteria for genre classification: Annotation and granularity. In: Workshop on Text-based Information Retrieval (TIR-06). Conjunction with ECAI 2006, Riva del Garda, 2006." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR83" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1735">2006</a>) proposed “annotation by objective sources”. This means that she identified genre-specific web domains, such as e-shops, and considered all texts from the domain as automatically belonging to the same genre without any further manual annotation. Automatic annotation was also applied to texts that contained the name of the genre in the title. This approach is based on the idea that if a text originates from a web domain which specializes in publishing texts of one genre, this means that web users collectively consider the text to belong to this genre. This approach was recently taken up by Lepekhin and Sharoff (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Lepekhin, M., & Sharoff, S. (2021). Experiments with adversarial attacks on text genres. arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2107.02246
                  
                " href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR59" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1738">2021</a>) as well, who named it “natural annotation”.</p><p>If researchers opted to use an existing genre schema for performing automatic genre identification experiments, they most often chose those from the few openly available datasets. For instance, two earlier schemata, Genre-KI-04 (Eissen & Stein, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Zu Eissen, S.M., & Stein, B. (2004). Genre classification of web pages. (2006). Common criteria for genre classification: Annotation and granularity. In: Workshop on Text-based Information Retrieval (TIR-06). (2021). Enhancing the identification of web genres by combining internal and external structures. (2018). Open set evaluation of web genre identification. However, today, most AGI experiments, as well as new genre datasets, are based on the schemata of the Corpus of Online Registers of English (CORE) (Egbert et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e1766">2015</a>), the Functional Text Dimensions (FTD) approach (Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Sharoff, S. The datasets and their schemata are described in more details in the following section.</p><h3 class="c-article__sub-heading" id="Sec7"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">4.3 </span>Comparison of datasets</h3><p>An overview of genre-annotated datasets with information on their size, language, number of classes and hierarchy depth, annotation approach and availability is shown in Table <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="table anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Tab2">2</a>. This is reflected in genre schemata, which consist either of a large number of specific categories or a smaller number of broader genre classes.</p><p><i>The hierarchical genre collection (HGC)</i> (Stubbe & Ringlstetter, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Stubbe, A., & Ringlstetter, C. (2007). Recognizing genres. Towards a reference corpus of web genres: Proceedings." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR98" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3140">2007</a>) is one of the first datasets annotated with a hierarchical schema. The schema was devised following a combination of a top-down and bottom-up approach. It was based on the genre set proposed by Dewe et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1998" title="Dewe, J., Karlgren, J., & Bretan, I. (1998). Assembling a balanced corpus from the internet. In: Proceedings of the 11th Nordic Conference of Computational Linguistics (NODALIDA 1998), pp. 100–108." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR23" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3143">1998</a>) and improved based on the feedback from a user study. The schema, shown in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Fig4">4</a>, consists of 7 main categories and 32 sub-categories. The dataset was collected manually, which means that it is a designed corpus, and consists of 1,280 texts that are prototypical for the assigned genre classes.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-4" data-title="Fig. 4"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig4" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 4</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><img aria-describedby="figure-4-desc" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs10579-023-09695-8/MediaObjects/10579_2023_9695_Fig4_HTML.png" alt="Fig. 4" loading="lazy" width="685" height="242"></picture><div class="c-article-section__figure-link"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="article-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8/figures/4" data-track-dest="link:Figure4 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 4" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-4-desc"><p>Hierarchical schema, proposed by Stubbe and Ringlstetter (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Stubbe, A., & Ringlstetter, C. (2007). Recognizing genres. Towards a reference corpus of web genres: Proceedings." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR98" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3159">2007</a>) and used in The hierarchical genre collection (HGC)</p></div></div></figure></div><p>The <i>KRYS I</i> (Berninger et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2008" title="Berninger, V.F., Kim, Y., & Ross, S. (2008). Building a document genre corpus: a profile of the KRYS I corpus. BCS-IRSG Workshop on Corpus Profiling, pp. 1–10." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR9" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3176">2008</a>) dataset consists of over 6,000 texts that are exclusively in the PDF format. The authors used their own hierarchical schema of 10 main categories and 70 subcategories, such as <i>Poetry Book, Menu, News Report, Contract, Essay, Sheet Music</i>. The dataset was collected manually by the students who collected instances of a genre that was assigned to them. Later, the instances were reclassified independently by two annotators.</p><p>The <i>SANTINIS-ML</i> dataset (Santini, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Santini, M. (2010). Cross-testing a genre classification model for the web. Genres on the Web (pp. 87–128). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR85" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3188">2010</a>) is a multi-label extension of the 7-Web Genre Collection (Santini, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Santini, M. (2007). Automatic identification of genre in web pages (Unpublished doctoral dissertation). University of Brighton." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR84" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3191">2007</a>). Here, the authors introduced a double-layered genre schema with the aim of being able to cover all of the diversity of texts found on the web without having a very high granularity. The schema consists of four functional genres (<i>Descriptive-Narrative, Explicatory-Informational, Argumentative-Persuasive</i> and <i>Instructional</i>) and 11 specific genre categories – the labels from the 7-Web Genre Collection and 4 BBC web genres (<i>Editorials, DIY Mini-Guides, Short Biographies, Feature Articles</i>). The dataset consists of 2,480 texts, annotated by the author of the research.</p><p>The <i>I-EN-Sample</i> and <i>I-RU-Sample</i> (Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S. (2010). In the garden and in the jungle genres on the web (pp. 149–166). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR88" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3214">2010</a>) datasets consist of 250 texts, annotated with the Functional Genre Classification schema. The schema consists of 7 macro-genres: <i>Discussion, Information, Instruction, Propaganda, Recreation, Regulation</i>, and <i>Reporting</i>. They are defined solely based on the function or the purpose of the document and the 7 of them should be able to cover all the texts on the web. The novelty of this approach lies in the fact that the schema aims for a high coverage with a low granularity by using broad functional categories. The dataset was collected based on the results of random queries made to a search engine.</p><p>The <i>CORE</i> dataset (Egbert et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Davies, M. (2015). Developing a bottom-up, user-based method of web register classification. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(9), 1817–1831." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR24" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3229">2015</a>) is the result of one of the most extensive works on the genre schema and annotation process. The CORE schema was constructed following the bottom-up approach, where the end web users were asked to provide situational characteristics of web texts that would be relevant for them. The initial schema was then improved based on a series of 10 pilot studies. The final schema as it is used in the dataset which is available online consists of 8 higher-level categories that cover the situational characteristics or functions of texts and 47 specific subcategories. The schema is shown in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Fig5">5</a>. A slightly modified schema with a smaller set of categories was used for annotation of Finnish (Laippala et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2019" title="Laippala, V., Kyllönen, R., Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Pyysalo, S. (2019). Toward multilingual identification of online registers. In: Proceedings of the 22nd Nordic Conference on Computational Linguistics, pp. 292–297." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR50" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3235">2019</a>; Skantsi & Laippala, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2023" title="Skantsi, V., & Laippala, V. (2023). Analyzing the unrestricted web: The finnish corpus of online registers. Nordic Journal of Linguistics, 1, 1–31." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR92" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3238">2023</a>), French and Swedish (Laippala et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2020" title="Laippala, V., Rönnqvist, S., Hellström, S., Luotolahti, J., Repo, L., Salmela, A., & Pyysalo, S. (2020). From web crawl to clean register-annotated corpora. In: Proceedings of the 12th Web as Corpus Workshop, pp. 14–22." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR52" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3242">2020</a>; Repo et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Repo, L., Skantsi, V., Rönnqvist, S., Hellström, S., Oinonen, M., Salmela, A., & Laippala, V. In: 16th Conference of the European Chapter of the Associationfor Computational Linguistics: Student Research Workshop, EACL 2021, pp. 183–191." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR77" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3245">2021</a>) datasets, for which the detailed guidelines are available.<sup><a href="#Fn4"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>4</a></sup> For the purposes of evaluation of a genre classifier model, 8 more datasets were recently annotated with CORE labels: an Indonesian dataset of around 1,000 texts, and 7 smaller evaluation datasets of 92 to 334 texts for Arabic, Catalan, Chinese, Hindi, Portuguese, Spanish and Urdu (see Laippala et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2022b" title="Laippala, V., Salmela, A., Rönnqvist, S., Aji, A.F., Chang, L.-H., Dhifallah, A., & Skantsi, V. In: Proceedings of the eighth workshop on noisy user-generated text (w-nut 2022), pp. 215–221." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR53" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3261">2022b</a>)).</p><p>The CORE corpus consists of web texts that were extracted from the “General” part of the Corpus of Global Web-based English (GloWbE) (Davies & Fuchs, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Davies, M., & Fuchs, R. (2015). Expanding horizons in the study of World Englishes with the 1.9 billion word Global Web-based English Corpus (GloWbE). English World-Wide, 36(1), 1–28." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR21" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3267">2015</a>). The GloWbE corpus was collected via Google searches with high frequency English 3-grams as the queries (Davies & Fuchs, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Davies, M., & Fuchs, R. (2015). Expanding horizons in the study of World Englishes with the 1.9 billion word Global Web-based English Corpus (GloWbE). English World-Wide, 36(1), 1–28." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR21" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3270">2015</a>). The texts were then annotated via crowd-sourcing with 908 participants, where each text was annotated by 4 annotators. Despite leading the annotators through the decision process with a decision-tree survey, the inter-annotator agreement was shown to be low (see Sect. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="section anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Sec6">4.2</a> for more details). The instances where there was no majority agreement on one label are annotated with multiple labels. The size of the dataset, as reported by the authors, is 53,000 texts, however, the dataset that is available online contains 48,420 texts. The dataset was used in further studies which provide a detailed analysis of linguistic characteristics of the CORE genres (Biber & Egbert, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Biber, D., & Egbert, J. (2018). Register variation online. Cambridge University Press." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR12" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3276">2018</a>), analyse the role of lexical and grammatical features in the performance and stability of genre classifiers (Laippala et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Laippala, V., Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Kyröläinen, A.-J. Language Resources and Evaluation, 5, 1–32." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR54" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3279">2021</a>), or experiment with automatic genre classification (Ronnqvist et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Rönnqvist, S., Skantsi, V., Oinonen, M., & Laippala, V. (2021). Multilingual and zero-shot is closing in on monolingual web register classification. The figure was created based on the information that was provided to us by the dataset authors</p></div></div></figure></div><p>The Slovene <i>Genre Identification Corpus (GINCO)</i> (Kuzman et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2022b" title="Kuzman, T., Rupnik, P., & Ljubešić, N. (2022). The GINCO training dataset for web genre identification of documents out in the wild. Proceedings of the language resources and evaluation conference (pp. 1584–1594). European Language Resources Association." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR47" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3316">2022b</a>) consists of 1,002 texts and uses a schema that is based on the subcategory level of the CORE schema, but also on other high-coverage schemata. In contrast to the CORE schema, it is not hierarchical and it has a lower granularity of categories to improve the inter-annotator agreement. The schema, shown in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Fig6">6</a>, consists of 23 specific genre categories and the category <i>Other</i>, dedicated to texts which do not fall into any other label. To alleviate the annotation, the genre categories were presented in category groups. The dataset was annotated by 2 expert annotators. They followed a multi-labelling approach where texts can be annotated with up to three genre labels. In this setting, the primary label is deemed to be the one that is most prevalent and the one that is used for single-label text classification, whereas the secondary and tertiary labels provide additional information on the fuzziness of the text, and the three levels can be used for multi-label classification. Extensive guidelines are available.<sup><a href="#Fn5"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>5</a></sup> The dataset is a crawled corpus, as it is randomly sampled from two Slovenian web corpora from different time periods – the slWaC 2.0 corpus (Erjavec & Ljubešić, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2014" title="Erjavec, T., & Ljubešić, N. (2014). The slwac 2.0 corpus of the slovene web. T. Erjavec, J. Žganec Gros (ur.). Jezikovne tehnologije zbornik, 17, 50–55." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR25" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3339">2014</a>) from 2014 and the MaCoCu-sl 1.0 corpus from a 2021 crawl (Bañón et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2022b" title="Bañón, M., Esplà-Gomis, M., Forcada, M.L., García-Romero, C., Kuzman, T., Ljubešić, N., & Zaragoza, J. (2022). Slovene web corpus MaCoCu-sl 1.0. (Slovenian language resource repository CLARIN.SI)" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR7" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3342">2022b</a>). To be representative of the conditions on the web, it also includes noise, that is, a subset of “not suitable” texts, such as non-textual documents and automatically generated documents, multi-genre documents and other web-specific challenges.</p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-6" data-title="Fig. 6"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig6" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 6</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><img aria-describedby="figure-6-desc" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs10579-023-09695-8/MediaObjects/10579_2023_9695_Fig6_HTML.png" alt="Fig. 6" loading="lazy" width="685" height="224"></picture><div class="c-article-section__figure-link"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="article-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8/figures/6" data-track-dest="link:Figure6 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 6" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-6-desc"><p>The GINCO schema</p></div></div></figure></div><p>The <i>Functional Text Dimensions</i> (FTD) dataset (Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Sharoff, S. (2018). Functional text dimensions for the annotation of web corpora. Corpora, 13(1), 65–95." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR89" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3368">2018</a>) in English and Russian follows another approach, introducing 18 Functional Text Dimensions (FTDs). As stated by the authors, the novelty of this approach is that “[u]nlike the traditional approach to designing genre lists or hierarchies in which texts need to be members of the respective classes, the FTD approach to detecting the genre of annotated texts is based on their similarity to prototypes, which is measured as distance in the FTD space” (Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Sharoff, S. (2018). Functional text dimensions for the annotation of web corpora. Corpora, 13(1), 65–95." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR89" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3371">2018</a>). The schema is a set of broad functional categories instead of specific labels, so that a text can be described through a combination of multiple labels, which could be regarded as parameters. By providing a possibility of assigning multiple labels to a text, the schema also deals with hybrid texts. In this approach, annotators define the presence of each dimension on a scale from 0 to 2, representing the distance of the text from the prototypical texts based on presence or absence of text features, typical for the genre class. As shown in Fig. <a data-track="click" data-track-label="link" data-track-action="figure anchor" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#Fig7">7</a>, the schema consists of 12 principal categories, which means that a text needs to be given a non-zero score in at least one of them, and 6 additional categories, which describe additional variation between texts. While the principal categories differentiate texts based on their function, additional categories provide information on other textual characteristics, for instance, on the stylistic differences, such as is the case of category <i>informal</i>, used for texts, written in informal language.</p><p>The FTD dataset consists of texts from multiple sources: the Pentaglossal corpus (5 g) (Forsyth & Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2014" title="Forsyth, R. S., & Sharoff, S. (2014). Document dissimilarity within and across languages: A benchmarking study. Literary and Linguistic Computing, 29(1), 6–22." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR29" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3383">2014</a>), which consists of Russian and English texts with known origin (fiction, corporate communication, political debates, TED talks, UN reports, etc.), and a random selection of texts from the ukWac web corpus (Baroni et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2009" title="Baroni, M., Bernardini, S., Ferraresi, A., & Zanchetta, E. (2009). The WaCky wide web: A collection of very large linguistically processed web-crawled corpora. Language Resources and Evaluation, 43(3), 209–226." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR8" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3386">2009</a>) and the Russian GICR web corpus (Piperski et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2013" title="Piperski, A., Belikov, V., Kopylov, N., Selegey, V., & Sharoff, S. (2013). Big and diverse is beautiful: A large corpus of Russian to study linguistic variation. In: Proceedings of 8th Web as Corpus Workshop (WAC-8), pp. 24–29." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR71" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3389">2013</a>). The FTD schema was extended to Arabic (Bulygin & Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Bulygin, M., & Sharoff, S. (2018). Using machine translation for automatic genre classification in Arabic. Komp’juternaja Lingvistika i Intellektual’nye Tehnologii, pp. 153–162." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR14" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3392">2018</a>), a smaller set of FTDs was used for annotation experiments of additional English datasets (Suchomel, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2020" title="Suchomel, V. (2020). Genre Annotation of Web Corpora: Scheme and Issues. In: Proceedings of the Future Technologies Conference, pp. 738–754." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR101" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3395">2020</a>), and a modified schema, consisting of 10 FTD labels, was used for annotation of a large Russian corpus, the <i>LiveJournal</i> dataset (Lepekhin & Sharoff, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2022" title="Lepekhin, M., & Sharoff, S. (2022). Estimating confidence of predictions of individual classifiers and their ensembles for the genre classification task. Proceedings of the language resources and evaluation conference (pp. 5974–5982). European Language Resources Association." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR60" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3402">2022</a>). Guidelines for annotation are available.<sup><a href="#Fn6"><span class="u-visually-hidden">Footnote </span>6</a></sup></p><div class="c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item" data-test="figure" data-container-section="figure" id="figure-7" data-title="Fig. 7"><figure><figcaption><b id="Fig7" class="c-article-section__figure-caption" data-test="figure-caption-text">Fig. 7</b></figcaption><div class="c-article-section__figure-content"><div class="c-article-section__figure-item"><picture class="c-article-section__figure-picture"><img aria-describedby="figure-7-desc" src="//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs10579-023-09695-8/MediaObjects/10579_2023_9695_Fig7_HTML.png" alt="Fig. 7" loading="lazy" width="685" height="125"></picture><div class="c-article-section__figure-link"><a class="c-article__pill-button" data-test="article-link" data-track="click" data-track-label="button" data-track-action="view figure" href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8/figures/7" data-track-dest="link:Figure7 Full size image" aria-label="Full size image figure 7" rel="nofollow"><span>Full size image</span><svg width="16" height="16" focusable="false" role="img" aria-hidden="true" class="u-icon"><use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class="c-article-section__figure-description" data-test="bottom-caption" id="figure-7-desc"><p>The FTD schema</p></div></div></figure></div><h4 class="c-article__sub-heading c-article__sub-heading--small" id="Sec9"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">4.3.2 </span>Information retrieval datasets</h4><p>Information retrieval datasets were created with the aim to provide genre identification inside the search engine, so that the users would be able to find the texts more efficiently based on genre criteria. Thus, their schemata consist of categories that are deemed to be useful for the search engine users.</p><p>The <i>Genre-KI-04</i> (Eissen & Stein, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Zu Eissen, S.M., & Stein, B. (2004). Genre classification of web pages. In: Annual Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 256–269." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR109" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3448">2004</a>) dataset consists of 1,239 HTML files, annotated with a schema of 8 categories, devised based on a survey on genre usefulness (bottom-up approach). The schema consists of the following labels: <i>Help, Article, Discussion, Shop, Portrayal (non-priv), Portrayal (priv), Link Collection</i> and <i>Download</i>. Recently, the schema was used by Agrawal et al. (<a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2019" title="Agrawal, S., Sanagavarapu, L.M., & Reddy, Y.R. (2019). FACT-Fine grained assessment of web page CredibiliTy. In: TENCON 2019-2019 IEEE Region 10 Conference (TENCON), pp. 1088–1097." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR2" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3457">2019</a>) for assessing the credibility of web pages.</p><p>The <i>7-Web Genre Collection</i> (Santini, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Santini, M. (2007). Automatic identification of genre in web pages (Unpublished doctoral dissertation). University of Brighton." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR84" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3466">2007</a>), in some works also referenced as SANTINIS, consists of 1,400 texts. It is annotated with 7 genre labels that are exclusive to the web: <i>Blog, e-Shop, FAQs, Online Newspaper Front Page, List, Personal Home Page</i>, and <i>Search Page</i>. The dataset, consisting of 200 instances of each genre, was manually collected by the author of the research, following the criteria of “annotation by objective sources”.</p><p>The <i>20-Genre Collection</i> (MGC) (Vidulin et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2007" title="Vidulin, V., Luštrek, M., & Gams, M. (2007). Using genres to improve search engines. In: 1st International Workshop: Towards Genre-Enabled Search Engines: The Impact of Natural Language Processing, pp. 45–51." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR105" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3481">2007</a>) consists of 1,539 texts. They are classified into 20 genres: <i>Blog, Childrens’, Commercial/Promotional, Community, Content Delivery, Entertainment, Error message, FAQ, Gateway, Index, Informative, Journalistic, Official, Personal, Poetry, Pornographic, Prose fiction, Scientific, Shopping</i>, and <i>User Input</i>. As the aim of the research was to construct a genre classifier which would identify genres within a search engine, the schema includes categories which would be of interest to the search engine users or which the users would want to filter out, e.g., the <i>Error message</i>. Based on the collection method, the corpus has both characteristics of a designed as well as a random corpus: first, instances were retrieved based on the searches made to the Google search engine using popular keywords. Secondly, the collection was enlarged by adding random web pages, and finally, instances of less frequent genre categories were manually collected to obtain a balanced corpus. The collection was one of the firsts that opted for the multi-labelling approach. Recently, the schema was transformed into a hierarchical set of categories, which was shown to improve the automatic genre prediction (Madjarov et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2019" title="Madjarov, G., Vidulin, V., Dimitrovski, I., & Kocev, D. (2019). Web genre classification with methods for structured output prediction. Information Sciences, 503, 551–573." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR64" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3494">2019</a>).</p><h4 class="c-article__sub-heading c-article__sub-heading--small" id="Sec10"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">4.3.3 </span>Other datasets</h4><p>The <i>Leeds Web Genre Corpus</i> (Asheghi et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2016" title="Asheghi, N. R., Sharoff, S., & Markert, K. (2016). Crowdsourcing for web genre annotation. Language Resources and Evaluation, 50(3), 603–641." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR5" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3509">2016</a>) is one of the largest English genre datasets, consisting of almost 5,000 texts. The dataset consists of two subcorpora, created with the aim of evaluating the proposed method for manual annotation: a balanced, manually collected subcorpus, and a random subcorpus, collected based on the automated queries made to a search engine. The balanced subcorpus was used to test the reliability of the manual annotation on a more controlled set of texts, and then the annotation campaign was extended to the random subcorpus to test the method in realistic conditions. The authors devised their own schema, constructed following the top-down approach, starting from the Genre-KI-04 schema (Eissen & Stein, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2004" title="Zu Eissen, S.M., & Stein, B. (2004). Genre classification of web pages. In: Annual Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 256–269." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR109" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3512">2004</a>). The schema consists of 20 specific genres, i.e., <i>Personal Homepage, Company/Business Homepage, Educational Organizational Homepage, Personal Blog/Diary, Online Shops, Instruction/How to, Recipe, News Article, Editorial, Conversational Forum, Biography, Frequently Asked Questions, Review, Interview, Story, Dictionary/Thesaurus Entries, Link Lists or Directories of Links, Song Lyrics, Quotes</i> and <i>Encyclopedic Articles</i>. The categories were shown to be able to cover 74% of the texts in the Leeds Corpus, while the remaining were annotated with the category <i>Other</i>. Despite the fact that the introduction of the category <i>Other</i> allows classification of any web text with the Leeds schema, the authors state that their main focus was not on “completeness of the genre inventory but on genre annotation methodology”. Since the authors note that the aim behind the construction of the dataset and the corresponding schema is not to provide a high-coverage schema, but to analyse genre annotation, we do not include the Leeds Web Genre Corpus under high-coverage collections, but rather describe it separately. The dataset was annotated via crowd-sourcing where each text was annotated by 5 participants. The annotation campaign was shown to be successful and a high inter-annotator agreement was reported, with the percentage agreement of 88% and Fleiss’ kappa (Fleiss, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1971" title="Fleiss, J. L. (1971). Measuring nominal scale agreement among many raters. Psychological Bulletin, 76(5), 378." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR28" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3528">1971</a>) of 0.87 on the balanced subcorpus, and the percentage agreement of 78% and Fleiss’ kappa of 0.71 on the random subcorpus.</p></div></div></section><section data-title="Automatic genre identification"><div class="c-article-section" id="Sec11-section"><h2 class="c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item" id="Sec11"><span class="c-article-section__title-number">5 </span>Automatic genre identification</h2><div class="c-article-section__content" id="Sec11-content"><p>Genre researchers used various technologies for automatic genre identification, mostly depending on the state-of-the-art of machine learning algorithms at the time of research. In the past, support vector machines (SVMs) were most frequently used (Rezapour Asheghi, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Rezapour Asheghi, N. (2015). Human annotation and automatic detection of web genres (Unpublished doctoral dissertation). University of Leeds." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR78" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3541">2015</a>; Laippala et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2017" title="Laippala, V., Luotolahti, J., Kyröläinen, A.-J., Salakoski, T., & Ginter, F. (2017). Creating register sub-corpora for the Finnish Internet Parsebank. In: Proceedings of the 21st Nordic Conference on Computational Linguistics, pp. 152–161." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR51" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3544">2017</a>, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2021" title="Laippala, V., Egbert, J., Biber, D., & Kyröläinen, A.-J. (2021). Exploring the role of lexis and grammar for the stable identification of register in an unrestricted corpus of web documents. Language Resources and Evaluation, 5, 1–32." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR54" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3547">2021</a>; Sharoff et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S., Wu, Z., & Markert, K. (2010). The Web Library of Babel: Evaluating genre collections. Lrec." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR90" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3550">2010</a>; Pritsos & Stamatatos, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Pritsos, D., & Stamatatos, E. (2018). Open set evaluation of web genre identification. Language Resources and Evaluation, 52(4), 949–968." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR73" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3553">2018</a>; Petrenz & Webber, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2011" title="Petrenz, P., & Webber, B. (2011). Stable classification of text genres. Computational Linguistics, 37(2), 385–393." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR70" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3557">2011</a>), as it was shown that they are very suitable for text categorization (Joachims, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1998" title="Joachims, T. (1998). Text categorization with support vector machines: Learning with many relevant features. European conference on machine learning (pp. 137–142). Springer." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR35" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3560">1998</a>). Other methods, previously used for genre classification, are the discriminant analysis (Feldman et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2009" title="Feldman, S., Marin, M.A., Ostendorf, M., & Gupta, M.R. (2009). Part-of-speech histograms for genre classification of text. In: 2009 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing, pp. 4781–4784." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR26" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3563">2009</a>; Biber & Egbert, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2015" title="Biber, D., & Egbert, J. (2015). Using grammatical features for automatic register identification in an unrestricted corpus of documents from the open web. Journal of Research Design and Statistics in Linguistics and Communication Science, 2(1), 3–36." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR11" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3566">2015</a>) which is the earliest method that was applied to this task (Karlgren & Cutting, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 1994" title="Karlgren, J., & Cutting, D. (1994). Recognizing text genres with simple metrics using discriminant analysis. In: Proceedings of the 15th International Conference on Computational Linguistics." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR39" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3569">1994</a>), decision tree classifiers, more specifically the C4.5 algorithm (Finn & Kushmerick, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2006" title="Finn, A., & Kushmerick, N. (2006). Learning to classify documents according to genre. Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 57(11), 1506–1518." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR27" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3572">2006</a>; Dewdney et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2001" title="Dewdney, N., Van Ess-Dykema, C., & MacMillan, R. (2001). The form is the substance: Classification of genres in text. In: Proceedings of the ACL 2001 Workshop on Human Language Technology and Knowledge Management." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR22" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3576">2001</a>), Naive Bayes algorithm (Feldman et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2009" title="Feldman, S., Marin, M.A., Ostendorf, M., & Gupta, M.R. (2009). Part-of-speech histograms for genre classification of text. In: 2009 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing, pp. 4781–4784." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR26" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3579">2009</a>; Priyatam et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2013" title="Priyatam, P. N., Iyengar, S., Perumal, K., & Varma, V. (2013). Don’t use a lot when little will do: Genre identification using URLs. Research in Computing Science, 70, 233–243." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR74" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3582">2013</a>) and graph-based models using hyper-link connections between web pages (Asheghi et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2014" title="Asheghi, N.R., Markert, K., & Sharoff, S. (2014). Semi-supervised graph-based genre classification for web pages. In: Proceedings of TextGraphs-9: The Workshop on Graph-Based Methods for Natural Language Processing, pp. 39–47." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR4" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3585">2014</a>; Zhu et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2011" title="Zhu, J., Zhou, X., & Fung, G. (2011). Enhance web pages genre identification using neighboring pages. In: International Conference on Web Information Systems Engineering, pp. 282–289." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR108" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3588">2011</a>). (2021). Exploring the role of lexis and grammar for the stable identification of register in an unrestricted corpus of web documents. Language Resources and Evaluation, 5, 1–32." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR54" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3591">2021</a>; Sharoff et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2010" title="Sharoff, S., Wu, Z., & Markert, K. (2010). The Web Library of Babel: Evaluating genre collections. Lrec." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR90" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3595">2010</a>; Pritsos & Stamatatos, <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2018" title="Pritsos, D., & Stamatatos, E. (2018). Open set evaluation of web genre identification. Language Resources and Evaluation, 52(4), 949–968." href="/article/10.1007/s10579-023-09695-8#ref-CR73" id="ref-link-section-d16177480e3598">2018</a>; Asheghi et al., <a data-track="click" data-track-action="reference anchor" data-track-label="link" data-test="citation-ref" aria-label="Reference 2014" title="Asheghi, N.R., Markert, K., & Sharoff, S.
